howto.name: How to prepare for the Colorado ADMT and chatbot rules

steps.name: Decide whether you are covered
steps.text: Test each AI system that touches a consequential decision in Colorado against the proposed materially influences threshold, and each consumer chatbot against the companionship and business exemptions.

steps.name: Retire SB 24-205 language
steps.text: Replace duty of reasonable care provisions in policies and contracts with the ADMT Act's disclosure, adverse outcome notice, human review and correction duties.

steps.name: Comment by October 26
steps.text: File written comments through the Department of Law's portal before 11:59 p.m. MT, or speak at the hearing.

steps.name: Plan for January 1, 2027
steps.text: Build the notices, review process, age assurance and annual reporting the final rules will require.

short: The Colorado Attorney General's proposed rules for the ADMT Act and the Chatbot Safety Act: the timeline, what the rules do, how to comment before the October 26, 2026 hearing, and what changed from SB 24-205.
title: Colorado ADMT and Chatbot Safety Rulemaking
subtitle: The rules for SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, hearing October 26, 2026
body_html:
On this page

  • Where it stands
  • The timeline
  • What the proposed rules do
  • How to comment
  • What changed from SB 24-205
  • Sources

Colorado is writing the rules for its two 2026 AI statutes now. The Attorney General filed one combined set of proposed rules, the Automated Decision-Making Technology and Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Rules at 4 CCR 904-6, on August 11, 2026. They implement SB 26-189, the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act, which repealed and replaced the 2024 Colorado AI Act, and HB 26-1263, the Chatbot Safety Act. Both statutes, and the rules once final, take effect January 1, 2027. This page tracks the rulemaking until it closes; the site's Colorado AI Act page covers the statutes.

Where it stands

The formal comment period is open and closes on October 26, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Mountain time, the same day as the public rulemaking hearing in Denver, held in person and by videoconference. If the hearing runs past that day, the comment period stays open through its last day. The rules are proposed, not final: anything in them can still change at or after the hearing.

The timeline

DateStep
May 2026Governor Polis signs SB 26-189 (May 14) and HB 26-1263
June 23 to July 13, 2026Informal pre-rulemaking comment period
August 11, 2026Proposed rules, notice of hearing and statement of basis filed with the Secretary of State; formal comment portal opens
September 4, 2026Deadline for comments to be considered in a revised draft
By September 23, 2026Any interim revised draft to be posted, according to the notice of hearing. Whether one was posted has not been confirmed on the Attorney General's page for this tracker
October 26, 2026Public rulemaking hearing, Denver and by videoconference; written comments close at 11:59 p.m. MT
January 1, 2027SB 26-189, HB 26-1263 and the final rules take effect

What the proposed rules do

For the ADMT Act. The rules set out when an automated decision-making technology "materially influences" a consequential decision, the threshold that decides whether a company is a covered developer or deployer; extend obligations to midstream developers; specify what a disclosure after an adverse outcome must contain; define what "meaningful human review" requires; and set the reporting duties and the process for consumers to request and correct inaccurate personal data used by the technology. Consequential decisions cover employment, lending, housing, insurance, health care, education and government services.

For the Chatbot Safety Act. The rules define which conversational AI services are "designed to simulate emotional companionship," which business-focused services are exempt, and what counts as commercially reasonable age assurance, disfavouring self-declared age or a government ID as the only method. They add detail on disclosures, protections for minors, crisis response, safeguards against prohibited content and the content of the operator's annual report. Rulemaking was mandatory under the ADMT Act and discretionary under the Chatbot Safety Act; the Attorney General chose to cover both in one package.

How to comment

Written comments go through the Colorado Department of Law's comment portal for the ADMT Act and Chatbot Safety Act, linked from its AI rulemaking page, until 11:59 p.m. MT on October 26, 2026. Comments at this stage enter the official rulemaking record. The hearing on October 26 takes oral comment in person in Denver or by videoconference; the notice of hearing on the Attorney General's page gives the room and joining details.

What changed from SB 24-205

SB 26-189 repealed and reenacted the 2024 Colorado AI Act before it ever took effect. The 2024 law's broad duty of reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination is gone; the new act is narrower, centred on automated decision-making technology that materially influences a consequential decision, with disclosure, notice after an adverse outcome, human review and consumer correction rights. Guidance, contracts and compliance programmes written to SB 24-205's duty of care need revising against the new statute and these rules.

Sources

  • Notice of rulemaking hearing and statement of basis, authority and purpose, filed August 11, 2026.
  • SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, Colorado General Assembly, 2026 regular session.
